citation: Explainable predictive models of short stature and exploration of related environmental growth factors: a case-control study. BMC Endocr Disord. 2025;25(1):125.
target_unit: log odds of normal-variant short stature
your_quote: Nighttime sleep duration (OR = 0.48, 95% CI: 0.26, 0.89) indicates that adequate sleep can also facilitate height growth, suggesting that children who get sufficient sleep have better growth outcomes compared to those who do not.
your_note: Source: PMC12067680 full text. Multivariate conditional logistic regression, Table 6: "Night sleep (24 h) | 0.72 (0.52, 1.01) | 0.06 | 0.48 (0.26, 0.89) | 0.02" (univariate then multivariate). Arithmetic: log_or = ln(0.48) = -0.733969; se = (ln(0.89) - ln(0.26))/3.92 = (-0.116534 + 1.347074)/3.92 = 0.313913. n = 100 cases + 200 age-matched controls = 300. AMBIGUITY 1 (design): this is a matched case-control study, which is not in the allowed design list; cross_sectional/TX is the nearest option. AMBIGUITY 2 (construct): the target label implies a dichotomous 'sufficient vs insufficient sleep' contrast, but in Table 6 the row 'Night sleep (24 h)' has no reference category, unlike the genuinely categorical rows in the same table which all show a 'No | 1' or 'Not at all | 1' reference row. The estimate therefore appears to be per unit (per hour) of night sleep, not sufficient-vs-insufficient. The narrative text describes it loosely as 'sufficient nighttime sleep duration'. AMBIGUITY 3 (sign): reported as the odds for MORE/sufficient sleep, hence negative. Harmonised to short sleep as the exposure (the stated 'positive = elevated risk with short sleep' convention, and target_exposure_type='habitual_short_sleep'), the value would be +0.733969 with the same SE. I report the contrast named by target_outcome_construct. Additional caveat: night sleep differed at p = 0.06 between cases (8.77 +/- 0.77 h) and controls (8.94 +/- 0.71 h), yet the stated variable-entry rule was p < 0.05, and the univariate OR (0.72) is far from the multivariate OR (0.48).

citation: Lee MR, Hwangbo Y, Kim JH, Yang KI, Hong SB. The association between weekend catch-up sleep and the reduction of obesity and overweight risk in adolescents with insufficient weekday sleep. Sleep and Breathing. 2025;29(2):184.
your_quote: Students with 3 or more h of CUS had lower odds of being overweight/obesity (odds ratio = 0.67, 95% confidence interval: 0.57-0.80) compared to those with non-CUS.
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 40366483). Full text is subscription-only (Sleep Breath; no PMC deposit, Europe PMC reports 'Subscription required'), so I could not see the regression tables. Arithmetic: log_or = ln(0.67) = -0.400478; se = (ln(0.80) - ln(0.57))/3.92 = (-0.223144 + 0.562119)/3.92 = 0.086473. Target dose 3.0 h vs referent 0.0 h maps exactly onto the reported '3 or more h of CUS' vs 'non-CUS' contrast. n = 12,434 high school students (total nationwide cross-sectional sample); the abstract does not state a category-specific analytic n, nor which covariates the logistic model adjusted for, so I cannot confirm this is the fully adjusted estimate. SIGN: as reported for the catch-up-sleep (more sleep) exposure, hence negative; equivalently, non-CUS (relatively shorter weekend sleep) carries elevated risk, so harmonised to a short-sleep exposure the value would be +0.400478.

citation: Sadikova E, Widome R, Robinson E, Aris IM, Tiemeier H. Delaying high school start times impacts depressed mood among students: evidence from a natural experiment. Soc Psychiatry Psychiatr Epidemiol. 2024 Nov;59(11):2073-2082.
target_unit: points on the 6-item Kandel-Davies depression scale (range 10-30, pooled baseline SD 5.00)
your_quote: We estimated a reduction in overall depression symptoms by 0.78, 95%CI (-1.32,-0.28) points over 2 years and a more pronounced impact on fatigue (-1.36 points, 95% CI (-2.19-0.69)), which likely drives the reductions in overall symptoms.
your_note: Source: PMC11846681 full text. Arithmetic: se = (-0.28 - (-1.32))/3.92 = 1.04/3.92 = 0.265306. Scale confirmed: 'The primary outcome was overall depression symptoms operationalized as the average of the individual item scores, multiplied by 10 for a final score ranging from 10 (no depression symptoms) to 30 (most severe symptoms)' - matches target_unit's stated 10-30 range. The abstract's '15.6% of a standard deviation' implies SD = 0.78/0.156 = 5.00, matching the target's stated pooled baseline SD of 5.00, so the raw-unit and SMD framings are mutually consistent. Sign negative = fewer depression symptoms under the ~0.5 h sleep GAIN (target 7.7 h vs 7.2 h referent, 730 days), i.e. sleep extension is beneficial. Estimation: g-estimation of a structural nested mean model using the school-start-time delay policy as the instrument; the paper's SEs were bootstrapped (1000 samples), but per protocol I derived the SE from the reported CI. n: 2,134 students enrolled (the figure the paper itself uses to describe the analysis); 2,054 fully completed the baseline survey and 1,917 contributed follow-up data, with censoring handled by stabilized IPCW - so the effective n for this estimate is somewhat below 2,134. Design: quasi_experiment is an equally defensible label (same tier T2); I chose instrumental_variable because the paper explicitly instruments individual sleep gain with the policy change. ROB moderate: not randomly assigned, only 5 clusters, unmeasured district-level confounding acknowledged by the authors.

citation: Cappuccio FP, D'Elia L, Strazzullo P, Miller MA. Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Sleep. 2010;33(5):585-592.
your_quote: Long duration of sleep (27 cohorts from 16 studies, n = 1,382,999 with 112,566 deaths) was associated with a greater risk of death (1.30; [1.22 to 1.38]; P < 0.0001) with no evidence of publication bias (P = 0.18)
your_note: Source: PMC2864873 full text (via the PMC article page; the Europe PMC/NCBI XML returned abstract only). Arithmetic: log = ln(1.30) = 0.262364; se = (ln(1.38) - ln(1.22))/3.92 = (0.322083 - 0.198851)/3.92 = 0.031437. SCALE MISMATCH: target_scale is 'log_hr' but the pooled estimate is a random-effects relative risk pooled from a mixture of RRs and HRs extracted from the primary studies; target_unit ('log relative risk') agrees with my reading, so I treated it as a log RR. TARGET-SPECIFICATION PROBLEM: target_exposure_type is 'habitual_short_sleep' but target_outcome_construct is 'all_cause_mortality_long_sleep_vs_normal'. I extracted the LONG-sleep estimate named by the construct. The corresponding short-sleep pooled RR is 1.12 (1.06-1.18), i.e. log 0.113, se 0.028, from 25 cohorts / 1,381,324 participants. Sign positive = elevated mortality with the named (long-sleep) exposure. Long sleep was mostly defined as >8 h/night; referent 7-8 h. Sleep assessed by questionnaire in all studies -> T5. ROB moderate: the authors themselves note that the long-sleep association 'may be explained by residual confounding and comorbidities'; substantial heterogeneity (P < 0.0001).

citation: Leproult R, Van Cauter E. Effect of 1 week of sleep restriction on testosterone levels in young healthy men. JAMA. 2011;305(21):2173-2174.
target_unit: % change in mean daytime total testosterone
your_quote: During waking hours common to both conditions (8 AM-10 PM), testosterone levels were lower after sleep restriction than in the rested condition (16.5 [2.8] nmol/L vs 18.4 [3.8] nmol/L; P = .049).
your_note: Source: PMC4445839 (NIH author manuscript) full text. The 8 AM-10 PM window is exactly the 0800-2200 daytime window named in target_outcome_construct. Arithmetic (value): pct_change = (16.5 - 18.4)/18.4 x 100 = -1.9/18.4 x 100 = -10.33%. Arithmetic (SE): the paper gives only between-subject SDs of each condition mean (2.8 and 3.8 nmol/L), not the SD of the within-subject paired difference, so I derived the SE from the p-value. Two-sided p = .049 -> z = 1.9686; SE of the mean difference = 1.9/1.9686 = 0.9652 nmol/L; on the percent scale, 0.9652/18.4 x 100 = 5.25 percentage points. CAVEAT: p came from a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, so the normal approximation is only approximate and this SE should be treated as indicative. Protocol matches the target: 3 nights of 10 h TIB (rested referent) then 8 nights of 5 h TIB (restriction) in 10 healthy young men. Alternative candidate values: the paper's own headline summary says 'Daytime testosterone levels were decreased by 10% to 15%'; the 2 PM-10 PM sub-window gives (15.5 - 17.9)/17.9 = -13.4%. I used the 8 AM-10 PM figure because it matches the named construct.

citation: Huang BH, Del Pozo Cruz B, Teixeira-Pinto A, Cistulli PA, Stamatakis E. Influence of poor sleep on cardiovascular disease-free life expectancy: a multi-resource-based population cohort study. BMC Med. 2023;21(1):75.
target_unit: CVD-free years lost at age 40, intermediate vs healthy sleepers, males
your_note: Source: PMC9979412 full text, Table 2 (columns are female CVD-free life expectancy, female years lost, male CVD-free life expectancy, male years lost). The abstract states the same: 'intermediate sleepers lost 0.48 [0.41-0.55] and 0.55 [0.49-0.61] years' for females and males respectively. Arithmetic: se = (0.61 - 0.49)/3.92 = 0.12/3.92 = 0.030612. Sign positive = CVD-free years LOST relative to healthy sleepers, at age 40, males. n = 308,683 UK Biobank participants in the self-reported core analysis (the 140,181 subsample is the primary-care-linkage analysis of clinical sleep disorders, not this estimate). EXPOSURE CAVEAT: the exposure is a 5-item composite sleep score (chronotype, duration, insomnia complaints, snoring, daytime sleepiness), with 'intermediate' = 2-3 healthy characteristics; target_exposure_type='habitual_short_sleep' captures only one of the five components. DESIGN AMBIGUITY: the underlying data are a prospective cohort with self-reported exposure (prospective_cohort_selfreport/T5 is defensible), but the estimand is a life-expectancy quantity from continuous-time three-state Cox Markov models, and the allowed tier list explicitly places 'life table' in TX, so I coded life_table/TX.

citation: Leproult R, Deliens G, Gilson M, Peigneux P. Beneficial impact of sleep extension on fasting insulin sensitivity in adults with habitual sleep restriction. Sleep. 2015;38(5):707-715.
your_quote: Indeed, total sleep time increased by 54 +/- 33 minutes over the 2 first weeks of the intervention, by 48 +/- 31 minutes over the 2 middle weeks of the intervention, and by 44 +/- 34 minutes over the 2 last weeks of the intervention (P <= 0.0001 for all comparisons to habitual time in bed and P > 0.25 for the comparisons between any 2-week periods of the intervention) without any significant change in sleep efficiency (P > 0.35).
your_note: Source: PMC4402666 full text (via the PMC article page). Arithmetic: 44 min / 60 = 0.733 h. SE: +/-34 is an SD (Figure 1 legend states 'Minutes of total sleep time (+SD)', and the reported individual range of -15 to +106 min for this block is consistent with SD ~= 34), so se = 34/sqrt(16)/60 = 8.5 min = 0.1417 h. AMBIGUITY - several candidate numbers exist for 'weekday TST gain from six-week sleep extension': (a) actigraphy, final 2 weeks: +44 +/- 34 min = 0.733 h [chosen, because this is the value the abstract headlines]; (b) actigraphy, first 2 weeks +54 +/- 33 min = 0.900 h; middle 2 weeks +48 +/- 31 min = 0.800 h; mean over all 6 weeks (54+48+44)/3 = 48.7 min = 0.811 h; (c) home PSG after 40 days: +49 +/- 68 min = 0.817 h (se 0.283 h); (d) self-reported sleep logs: 'increased by about 1 h'. n = 16 volunteers; actigraphy was missing for 2 participants in intervention weeks 1-2 and 1 in weeks 3-4, but not in weeks 5-6, so n = 16 for the chosen block. DESIGN CAVEAT: uncontrolled single-arm within-subject sleep extension conducted at home under real-life conditions, not in a laboratory; I used lab_restriction_within_subject/T1 as the only within-subject experimental option, but quasi_experiment/T2 is defensible.

citation: Zhao B, Meng Y, Jin X, Xi W, Ma Q, Yang J, Ma X, Yan B. Association of Objective and Self-Reported Sleep Duration With All-Cause and Cardiovascular Disease Mortality: A Community-Based Study. J Am Heart Assoc. 2023 Mar 21;12(6):e027832.
your_quote: multivariable Cox regression analysis found that objective sleep duration <=4 hours (hazard ratio [HR], 2.43 [95% CI, 1.83-3.22], P<0.001), 4 to 5 hours (HR, 1.66 [95% CI, 1.30-2.12], P<0.001), 5 to 6 hours (HR, 1.37 [95% CI, 1.10-1.71], P=0.005), and 6 to 7 hours (HR, 1.42 [95% CI, 1.15-1.76], P=0.001) were significantly associated with all-cause mortality compared with that of the reference (7-8 hours)
your_note: Source: PMC10111539 full text, Table 2 (fully adjusted model). Target dose 5.5 h maps to the '5-6 h' category and referent 7.5 h to the '7-8 h' reference category. Arithmetic: log_hr = ln(1.37) = 0.314811; se = (ln(1.71) - ln(1.10))/3.92 = (0.536493 - 0.095310)/3.92 = 0.112547. Sign positive = elevated mortality with shorter sleep, per convention. Adjusted for age, sex, race, BMI, smoking, alcohol, diabetes, hypertension, history of major CVD, chronic respiratory disease, lipid-lowering medication, benzodiazepine use, AHI and T90. n: 5,027 is the full SHHS analytic cohort on which the Cox model was fitted; the two cells specifically compared contain 1,396 (5-6 h, 349 deaths) and 855 (7-8 h, 115 deaths) = 2,251 participants, if a contrast-specific n is wanted. target_exposure_duration_days = 1 correctly reflects that exposure came from a single night of in-home PSG - the authors flag night-to-night variability as a limitation, which is the main reason for ROB moderate rather than low.

citation: Kitamura S, Katayose Y, Nakazaki K, Motomura Y, Oba K, Katsunuma R, Terasawa Y, Enomoto M, Moriguchi Y, Hida A, Mishima K. Estimating individual optimal sleep duration and potential sleep debt. Scientific Reports. 2016;6:35812.
target_unit: hours of total sleep time (individual optimal sleep duration, PSG)
your_quote: The mean estimated OSD was 8.41 +/- 0.18 h (range, 7.29-9.26 h).
your_note: Source: PMC5075948 full text. Protocol matches the target exactly: '9 consecutive days of extended sleep sessions (sessions E1-E9) with TIB set at 12 h', PSG-derived TST, n = 15. SE: I read +/-0.18 as an SEM, because 0.18 x sqrt(15) = 0.70 h implies an SD consistent with the reported 7.29-9.26 h range; if +/-0.18 were an SD the SE would instead be 0.18/sqrt(15) = 0.046. Method caveat: OSD was estimated by constrained exponential-decay curve fitting of nightly TST; the fit failed to converge for 2 of 15 participants (S05, S11), for whom the mean of their extended-sleep TSTs was substituted, and single nights were dropped for 3 participants for technical/low-efficiency reasons. Related quantities in the same paper that are NOT the target: habitual sleep duration 7.37 +/- 0.27 h, potential sleep debt 1.04 +/- 0.24 h, TST at E1 10.59 +/- 0.19 h. DESIGN NOTE: this is a descriptive sleep-need estimate rather than an exposure-outcome contrast, so normative_descriptive/TX is defensible; I used the parent within-subject lab extension design.

citation: Alvarez-Ornelas NA, Macias-Cervantes HE, Rodriguez-Villasenor P, Sanchez-Figueroa O, Flores-Rodriguez R, Garcia-Cisneros ZG, et al. Sleep deprivation as a risk factor for cortical gray matter reduction in new medical residents. Journal of Neuroradiology. 2025;52(4):101357.
your_quote: We found an OR of 1.52 (95 % CI 0.93-4.14, p = 0.01) between working night shifts and gray matter reduction.
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 40449887), corroborated verbatim on the publisher's abstract page (em-consulte). Journal of Neuroradiology full text is closed and not in PMC, so I could not see the regression table. Arithmetic: log_or = ln(1.52) = 0.418710; se = (ln(4.14) - ln(0.93))/3.92 = (1.420696 + 0.072571)/3.92 = 0.380935. SOURCE DEFECT: the reported interval is internally inconsistent. It includes 1.0 yet is reported with p = 0.01, and it is not centred on the point estimate on the log scale (ln 1.52 = 0.419; distance to ln 0.93 is 0.492, distance to ln 4.14 is 1.002). The protocol-mandated CI-based SE is 0.381; if p = 0.01 were instead correct the implied SE would be 0.419/2.576 = 0.163. That is a >2x discrepancy, so any inverse-variance weight for this estimate is unreliable. n = 41 newly admitted medical residents, each scanned at baseline and again 4 months later (matches target_exposure_duration_days = 120). Design: the OR is a within-cohort comparison of residents working night shifts vs not, i.e. observational; sleep exposure was captured by questionnaire, hence prospective_cohort_selfreport/T5. ROB high: tiny sample, no external control group, secular/scanner drift not addressed, exposure crudely dichotomised.

citation: Sun J, Zhao R, Yang X, Deng H, Zhu Y, Chen Y, Yuan K, Xi Y, Yin H, Qin W. Alteration of Brain Gray Matter Density After 24 h of Sleep Deprivation in Healthy Adults. Frontiers in Neuroscience. 2020;14:754.
your_quote: According to the results, /\GMD in the MFG and /\KSS scores showed significantly positive correlation, as shown in Figure 4 (Spearman's correlation r = 0.625, p = 0.0014, Bonferroni correction with p < 0.05/25).
your_note: Source: PMC7438917 full text (the delta symbol in the original is rendered here as /\ because the extracted text uses a non-ASCII triangle). Arithmetic: on the correlation scale, se = sqrt((1 - r^2)/(n - 2)) = sqrt((1 - 0.390625)/21) = sqrt(0.029018) = 0.170346. Consistency check: t = 0.625/0.170346 = 3.669, which at df = 21 gives two-sided p = 0.0014 - exactly the p reported - so the reported test used df = n - 2 = 21 even though the methods say age, sex and BMI were partialled out. If the Fisher-z scale is preferred, se_z = 1/sqrt(n - 3) = 0.224. n = 23 (25 recruited, 1 excluded for scanner failure, 1 withdrew during the SD session). Exposure: 24 h total sleep deprivation vs rested wakefulness in randomized crossover order, matching target dose 0 h / 1 day. INTERPRETATION CAVEAT: this is a correlation between the SD-induced change in gray matter density in the right middle frontal gyrus and the SD-induced change in Karolinska Sleepiness Scale score - not a treatment effect of deprivation on any outcome, and not signed in the 'worse outcome under restriction' sense. Note also the direction: GMD in the right MFG INCREASED after deprivation, so a positive r means a larger GMD increase accompanied a larger sleepiness increase. Multiplicity: this was 1 of 25 brain-region x behavioural-measure correlations tested.

citation: Al Khatib HK, Harding SV, Darzi J, Pot GK. The effects of partial sleep deprivation on energy balance: a systematic review and meta-analysis. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2017;71(5):614-624.
your_quote: The pooled mean increase in total 24-h EI in the PSD condition compared with control was 385 kcal (95% confidence interval (CI): 252, 517; P<0.00001), with low heterogeneity (Q = 6.28, d.f. = 10, P = 0.79, I2 = 0%)
your_note: Source: European Journal of Clinical Nutrition full text is closed; I used an author-deposited copy of the article (ResearchGate record for the same DOI) whose results section matches the PubMed abstract verbatim on the key figure (385 kcal; 95% CI 252, 517). Arithmetic: se = (517 - 252)/3.92 = 265/3.92 = 67.602. Sign positive = HIGHER energy intake under partial sleep deprivation (i.e. the adverse direction). n = 172 participants across the 11 studies with extractable data (of 17 in the review, n = 496). The body text reports the EI analysis as 185 PSD and 161 control observations across 11 comparisons (d.f. = 10), because one study contributed male and female strata separately and most designs were crossover. TARGET-SPECIFICATION PROBLEM: target_exposure_type = 'chronic_restriction' fits poorly. The pooled interventions were partial sleep deprivation protocols of mostly 1 to a few nights, and the task leaves dose, referent and duration null, so the pooled estimate averages heterogeneous restriction doses and durations. ROB some_concerns: 7 of the 11 contributing comparisons were randomized and 4 were not; the authors' sensitivity analysis gave 364 kcal (191, 538) for randomized and 411 kcal (165, 657) for non-randomized studies. Heterogeneity was low (I2 = 0%).

citation: Van Dongen HPA, Maislin G, Mullington JM, Dinges DF. The Cumulative Cost of Additional Wakefulness: Dose-Response Effects on Neurobehavioral Functions and Sleep Physiology From Chronic Sleep Restriction and Total Sleep Deprivation. Sleep. 2003;26(2):117-126.
your_quote: Significant differences among conditions in the rate of change across days (parameter beta in equation (1)) were found for psychomotor vigilance task performance (F2,30 = 3.67, P = 0.037), digit symbol substitution task performance (F2,30 = 5.33, P = 0.010), and serial addition/subtraction task performance (F2,30 = 6.19, P = 0.006).
your_note: NULL, not because the source is unavailable but because the requested quantity is not derivable from it. I retrieved the complete article text (author/institutional copy at med.upenn.edu/uep/assets/user-content/documents/VanDongen_etal_Sleep_26_2_2003.pdf; the OUP version is Cloudflare-blocked to non-browser clients). The paper contains NO tables of PVT lapse means or SDs, and reports no standardized effect size for any condition or day. All PVT results are presented either graphically (Figure 1A, lapses expressed relative to baseline) or as mixed-effects model parameters: the condition-specific rate-of-change beta, the omnibus F2,30 = 3.67 (P = 0.037) quoted above, curvature theta = 0.78 +/- 0.04 for the PVT, the critical wake period xi = 15.84 +/- 0.73 h, and the implied daily sleep need 24 - xi = 8.16 +/- 0.73 h. The omnibus F tests the difference in the RATE OF CHANGE across the 4/6/8 h arms, not a day-14 4 h vs 8 h level contrast, and cannot be converted into a Hedges' g for that contrast. Producing a g would require digitizing Figure 1A and supplying variance information the paper never reports, so any number I gave would be fabricated. your_n = 22 is the group-size sum for the requested contrast (4 h arm n = 13; 8 h arm n = 9); the full experiment was n = 48 across 4 h, 6 h, 8 h and 0 h arms. Design: participants were randomized to 8 h, 6 h or 4 h TIB for 14 days in parallel arms, so rct_parallel/T1. ROB some_concerns: randomized but unblinded, very small arms, and the 8 h arm was significantly younger than the 6 h arm (P = 0.022). FLAG: any non-null Hedges' g for this target most likely traces to a downstream meta-analysis (e.g. Lim & Dinges) rather than to the source paper; I deliberately did not import such a value.

citation: Howard C, Mukadam N, Hui EK, Livingston G. The effects of sleep duration on the risk of dementia incidence in short and long follow-up studies: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine. 2024 Dec;124:522-530. (Corrigendum: Sleep Medicine. 2025 May;129:131, doi 10.1016/j.sleep.2025.02.039, PMID 40022863.)
your_quote: Moreover, long follow-up studies (N = 515,698; 4 studies) showed a 74 % increased risk of dementia incidence in later life (RR - 1.74; 95 CIs 1.30-2.18).
your_note: Source: author-accepted manuscript of the original article in UCL Discovery (eprint 10198927), which reproduces the published text; ScienceDirect and PMC were not accessible. Arithmetic: log_rr = ln(1.74) = 0.553885; se = (ln(2.18) - ln(1.30))/3.92 = (0.779325 - 0.262364)/3.92 = 0.131878. Matches the target exactly: extended sleep duration (>= 9 h/night, target dose 9 h) and follow-up > 10 years. I2 = 86.56%. Sign positive = elevated dementia risk with LONG sleep, the named exposure. T5 because 28 of the 31 included studies used self-reported sleep duration (2 actigraphy, 1 PSG). ROB high: the authors rated 20/31 studies moderate risk and 10/31 high risk, with only 1 low risk, and describe the heterogeneity as limiting external validity. CORRIGENDUM CAVEAT: the article carries a 2025 corrigendum (Sleep Med 129:131, PMID 40022863) which has no abstract on PubMed and which I could not retrieve. The published abstract contains an obvious CI typo for a DIFFERENT estimate (brief sleep, short follow-up: abstract '1.48-1.77' vs body text '1.15-1.77' around a point estimate of 1.46), which is the most likely subject of the correction; but I cannot positively rule out that the corrigendum also revised the extended-sleep long-follow-up figure I extracted.

citation: Shan Z, Ma H, Xie M, Yan P, Guo Y, Bao W, Rong Y, Jackson CL, Hu FB, Liu L. Sleep duration and risk of type 2 diabetes: a meta-analysis of prospective studies. Diabetes Care. 2015 Mar;38(3):529-37.
target_unit: log RR per 1 h shorter sleep below 7 h/day
your_quote: Compared with 7-h sleep duration per day, the pooled relative risks for type 2 diabetes were 1.09 (95% CI 1.04-1.15) for each 1-h shorter sleep duration among individuals who slept <7 h per day and 1.14 (1.03-1.26) for each 1-h increment of sleep duration among individuals with longer sleep duration.
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 25715415), corroborated verbatim by the University of Iowa institutional record; Diabetes Care full text is closed and not in PMC. Arithmetic: log_rr = ln(1.09) = 0.086178; se = (ln(1.15) - ln(1.04))/3.92 = (0.139762 - 0.039221)/3.92 = 0.025648. Matches the target exactly: per 1 h SHORTER sleep among those sleeping < 7 h/day, referent 7 h. Sign positive = elevated risk with shorter sleep, per convention. n = 482,502 participants with 18,443 incident type 2 diabetes cases across 10 articles / 11 reports, follow-up 2.5-16 years; this is the review total. The number contributing specifically to the < 7 h arm of the U-shaped spline is not reported in the accessible abstract, so 482,502 may overstate the analytic n for this segment. T5: sleep duration was self-reported in the pooled prospective cohorts.

citation: Henry A, Katsoulis M, Masi S, Fatemifar G, Denaxas S, Acosta D, Garfield V, Dale CE. The relationship between sleep duration, cognition and dementia: a Mendelian randomization study. International Journal of Epidemiology. 2019 Jun 1;48(3):849-860.
your_quote: Similarly, we found no evidence of an association between sleep duration and the risk of AD in IGAP [ORIVW = 0.89 (95% CI = 0.67-1.18); P = 0.41].
your_note: Source: PMC6659373 full text. Arithmetic: log_or = ln(0.89) = -0.116534; se = (ln(1.18) - ln(0.67))/3.92 = (0.165514 + 0.400478)/3.92 = 0.144386. Units confirmed by the paper's table footnote: 'numbers represent effect size per additional hour/day in sleep duration'. TARGET-SPECIFICATION PROBLEM: target_outcome_construct says 'per_additional_hour_of_genetically_instrumented_sleep' while target_exposure_type says 'per_hour_less_sleep' - these are opposite directions. I report the contrast named by the construct (per additional hour), hence negative. Harmonised to per hour LESS sleep, per the stated 'positive = elevated risk with short sleep' convention, the value is +0.116534 with the same SE. This single sign decision flips the estimate and is the most likely source of disagreement on this row. n = 54,162 = IGAP stage I 17,008 AD cases + 37,154 controls (the outcome sample). The 77-SNP instrument was derived from UK Biobank N = 395,803. Primary estimator inverse-variance weighted. ROB moderate: very imprecise (CI spans 0.67-1.18), and the authors' own non-linear MR indicates the linear instrument is mis-specified for sleep duration.

citation: Blake MJ, Sheeber LB, Youssef GJ, Raniti MB, Allen NB. Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Adolescent Cognitive-Behavioral Sleep Interventions. Clin Child Fam Psychol Rev. 2017 Sep;20(3):227-249.
your_quote: There were a small number of randomized controlled trials (RCTs; n = 4) and a high risk of bias across the RCTs; therefore, within sleep condition meta-analyses were examined (n = 221). At post-intervention, subjective TST improved by 29.47 min (95% CI 17.18, 41.75), SOL by 21.44 min (95% CI -30.78, -12.11), SE by 5.34% (95% CI 2.64, 8.04), and WASO by a medium effect size [d = 0.59 (95% CI 0.36, 0.82)].
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 28331991), corroborated verbatim by the Springer/BSL abstract page. Full text is closed; the OpenAlex-listed green copy on figshare requires JavaScript and could not be retrieved. Arithmetic: se = (41.75 - 17.18)/3.92 = 24.57/3.92 = 6.268. Sign positive = MORE total sleep time after the intervention. MAJOR CAVEAT: this is a WITHIN-GROUP (pre- to post-intervention, uncontrolled) pooled change, not a randomized between-group contrast. The authors pooled within sleep condition precisely because there were only 4 RCTs and a high risk of bias across them, so this estimate conflates intervention effect with the passage of time, expectancy and regression to the mean. Tier T1 reflects the trial-based design label, but the estimate does not carry randomized-contrast strength. n = 221 is the total across the within-condition meta-analyses (9 trials, n = 357 overall); the k and n specific to the subjective-TST pooling are not in the accessible abstract. target_exposure_type='sleep_extension' is loose: the interventions were multicomponent cognitive-behavioural sleep programmes, not prescribed time-in-bed extension, and dose/referent/duration are all null in the task.

citation: Gradisar M, Dohnt H, Gardner G, Paine S, Starkey K, Menne A, Slater A, Wright H, Hudson JL, Weaver E, Trenowden S. A randomized controlled trial of cognitive-behavior therapy plus bright light therapy for adolescent delayed sleep phase disorder. Sleep. 2011;34(12):1671-1680.
target_unit: hours of school-night total sleep time
your_note: Source: PMC3208844 full text (via the PMC article page), Table 2: 'Pre- and post-treatment mean +/- SDs of sleep, sleepiness, and depression symptoms between DSPD adolescents undergoing CBT plus BLT (N = 23) or in a Waitlist (WL) control condition (N = 17)'. The four numeric columns are pre-treatment CBT+BLT, pre-treatment WL, post-treatment CBT+BLT, post-treatment WL. Because the target is descriptive (target_exposure_type='descriptive'), I pooled the two PRE-treatment arms: mean = (23 x 7.1 + 17 x 6.9)/40 = 280.6/40 = 7.015 h -> 7.02 h; pooled SD = sqrt((22 x 1.3^2 + 16 x 1.4^2)/38) = sqrt(68.54/38) = 1.343 h; se = 1.343/sqrt(40) = 0.2123 h. Measured by 7-day sleep diary, matching target_exposure_duration_days = 7. AMBIGUITY: other defensible readings are the CBT+BLT arm alone (7.1 +/- 1.3, n = 23), the waitlist arm alone (6.9 +/- 1.4, n = 17), or the untreated waitlist at post-treatment (6.9 +/- 1.1). All fall in 6.9-7.1 h, so the choice moves the value by at most ~0.1 h. DESIGN AMBIGUITY: the source study is an RCT (rct_parallel/T1), but the extracted quantity carries no randomized contrast, so I coded the estimand as normative_descriptive/TX and rob as na. If your_design is meant to describe the study rather than the estimand, rct_parallel/T1 applies.

citation: Cappuccio FP, Cooper D, D'Elia L, Strazzullo P, Miller MA. Sleep duration predicts cardiovascular outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Eur Heart J. 2011 Jun;32(12):1484-1492.
your_quote: In the pooled analysis, short duration of sleep was weakly and not significantly associated with a greater risk of developing or dying of total CVD (RR 1.03, 0.93-1.15, P = 0.52) with no evidence of publication bias (P = 0.46) and no heterogeneity between studies (I2 = 0%, Q = 3.42, P = 0.97) (Figure 3A).
your_note: Source: full text of the article from the authors' institutional copy at Warwick (warwick.ac.uk/.../ehj_2011_sleep__cvd.pdf); the OUP version is Cloudflare-blocked. Arithmetic: log_rr = ln(1.03) = 0.029559; se = (ln(1.15) - ln(0.93))/3.92 = (0.139762 + 0.072571)/3.92 = 0.054166. Sign positive = elevated risk with SHORT sleep, per convention (note the estimate is essentially null). n: the article text only gives review-level totals (474,684 participants, 24 cohorts, 16,067 events of which 8,420 total CVD); the per-analysis totals appear only inside the Figure 3A forest plot, which is not present in the extractable PDF text. The authors' own conference poster reproducing Figure 3A lists 11 cohorts for the short-sleep/total-CVD analysis totalling 222,253 participants and 8,250 total CVD events, which is consistent with Q = 3.42 at P = 0.97 (df ~= 10). I therefore used 222,253; if the whole-review figure is preferred instead, it is 474,684. This is the one number in this row I could not verify inside the article itself. T5: sleep duration was assessed by questionnaire in all included studies; short sleep mostly defined as <= 5-6 h/night with a 7-8 h referent.

citation: Zhang Y, Zhao W, Liu K, Chen Z, Fei Q, Ahmad N, Yi M. The causal associations of altered inflammatory proteins with sleep duration, insomnia and daytime sleepiness. Sleep. 2023;46(10):zsad207.
target_unit: MR estimate, genetically predicted CRP on sleep duration (units per the source GWAS)
your_quote: In MR analysis, the primary results demonstrated the causal effects of CRP on sleep duration (estimate: 0.017; 95% confidence intervals [CI], [0.003, 0.031]) and short sleep duration (estimate: -0.006; 95% CI, [-0.011, -0.001]).
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 37535878), corroborated verbatim by the publisher abstract page; Sleep full text is closed and not in PMC. Arithmetic: se = (0.031 - 0.003)/3.92 = 0.028/3.92 = 0.007143. DIRECTION: as the construct name states, this is the REVERSE direction - genetically predicted CRP acting on sleep duration. The outcome here is sleep duration, not a health outcome, so the 'positive = elevated risk with short sleep' convention does not apply and this estimate cannot serve as evidence about the effects OF sleep on anything. Positive simply means higher genetically predicted CRP is associated with longer sleep duration. I took the continuous 'sleep duration' estimate (0.017) rather than the companion binary 'short sleep duration' estimate (-0.006), because the construct says 'on_sleep_duration'. UNITS: whatever the source sleep-duration GWAS used (self-reported h/day per unit/SD of genetically predicted CRP); the abstract does not state them, consistent with target_unit's own hedge ('units per the source GWAS'). your_n = null deliberately: the MR used published GWAS summary statistics whose sample sizes are only in the paywalled methods. The 51,879 participants quoted in the abstract belong to the separate observational quantitative synthesis of 44 publications and are NOT the MR sample - using that number here would be wrong. Primary estimator was inverse-variance weighted with sensitivity analyses.

citation: Koopman ADM, Rauh SP, van 't Riet E, Groeneveld L, van der Heijden AA, Elders PJ, Dekker JM, Nijpels G, Beulens JW, Rutters F. The Association between Social Jetlag, the Metabolic Syndrome, and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in the General Population: The New Hoorn Study. Journal of Biological Rhythms. 2017;32(4):359-368.
your_quote: After adjustment for sex, employment status, and educational level, prevalence ratios of 1.15 (95% CI 0.9-1.5) were observed for participants with 1-2 h social jetlag and 1.64 (95% CI 1.1-2.4) for participants with >2 h social jetlag, compared with participants with <1 h social jetlag (p for trend = 0.04).
your_note: Source: PMC5564947 full text, Table 2 Model 2 (the paper's designated main model). Arithmetic: ln(1.64) = 0.494696; se = (ln(2.4) - ln(1.1))/3.92 = (0.875469 - 0.095310)/3.92 = 0.199020. SCALE MISMATCH (important): target_scale is 'log_or' but the paper reports PREVALENCE RATIOS from modified Poisson regression, chosen deliberately because 'the high prevalence of the metabolic syndrome would have led to overestimation of relative risks' with logistic regression. A PR of 1.64 at ~20% baseline prevalence corresponds to a materially larger OR, so treating ln(PR) as a log OR biases this estimate toward zero. DOSE MAPPING: the paper's categories are <1 h, 1-2 h and >2 h social jetlag. Target dose 2.0 h maps to '>2 h' (observed mean 139.6 +/- 24 min = 2.33 h) and referent 0.5 h to '<1 h' (observed mean 21.7 +/- 17 min = 0.36 h), so the task's contrast is approximate rather than exact. PRECISION: the published CIs are rounded to one decimal place (1.1-2.4), so the derived SE is coarse. MODEL CHOICE: I used the total-population Model 2. Model 4 (additionally adjusted for BMI) attenuates the association - the authors state it 'was confounded or mediated by BMI' - and the <61-year stratum gives a larger PR of 2.13 (1.3-3.4). n = 1,585. Cross-sectional -> TX; ROB high (single-time-point self-reported chronotype questionnaire, prevalent outcome, missing confounders imputed by mean substitution).

citation: Liang Y, Qu LB, Liu H. Non-linear associations between sleep duration and the risks of mild cognitive impairment/dementia and cognitive decline: a dose-response meta-analysis of observational studies. Aging Clinical and Experimental Research. 2019 Mar;31(3):309-320.
your_quote: The pooled RR per 1 h increases in sleep duration was 0.99 (95% CI 0.97-1.01, I2 = 62.40%, P = 0.02, n = 6) for cognitive decline risk, and 0.98 (95% CI 0.97-1.00, I2 = 0%, P = 0.42, n = 4) for MCI/dementia risk.
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 30039452), corroborated verbatim by the Springer abstract page; Aging Clin Exp Res full text is closed and not in PMC. I took the MCI/dementia figure, 0.98 (0.97-1.00), not the cognitive-decline figure 0.99 (0.97-1.01), per the construct. Arithmetic: log_rr = ln(0.98) = -0.020203; se = (ln(1.00) - ln(0.97))/3.92 = 0.030459/3.92 = 0.007770. SIGN: as reported, per ADDITIONAL hour of sleep, matching target_outcome_construct ('per_additional_hour_of_sleep_LINEAR_term'). Note that target_exposure_type says 'per_hour_less_sleep', which is the opposite direction; harmonised that way the value is +0.020203 with the same SE. Same sign-convention conflict as henry2019 and a likely disagreement source. your_n = null: the 'n = 4' in the quoted sentence is the number of STUDIES, not participants. The review-level totals (62,937 individuals, 2,718 MCI/dementia cases, 5,596 cognitive-decline cases) span all 9 included studies, and the abstract does not report how many participants the 4 MCI/dementia studies contributed, so neither 62,937 nor 2,718 is defensible as the analytic n for this estimate. TIER CAVEAT: the review mixed 5 prospective cohort with 4 cross-sectional studies and I cannot verify which 4 fed the linear MCI/dementia model; T5 assumes prospective, self-reported exposure, but TX would be correct if cross-sectional studies dominate that subset. ROB high for the same reason plus the near-null, essentially uninformative estimate combined with strong reported non-linearity (P_nonlinearity < 0.001), which makes a single linear term a poor summary.

citation: Benjafield AV, Ayas NT, Eastwood PR, Heinzer R, Ip MSM, Morrell MJ, et al. Estimation of the global prevalence and burden of obstructive sleep apnoea: a literature-based analysis. Lancet Respir Med. 2019;7(8):687-698.
your_quote: Using AASM 2012 diagnostic criteria and AHI threshold values of five or more events per h and 15 or more events per h, we estimated that 936 million (95% CI 903-970) adults aged 30-69 years (men and women) have mild to severe obstructive sleep apnoea and 425 million (399-450) adults aged 30-69 years have moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnoea globally.
your_note: Source: PMC7007763 full text; the body text repeats it as 'the corresponding figure for an AHI of 15 or more events per h was 425 million (399-450; figure 1)'. Value = 425 (millions of adults aged 30-69 worldwide with AHI >= 15, i.e. moderate-to-severe OSA under AASM 2012 criteria), matching target_unit exactly. Arithmetic: se = (450 - 399)/3.92 = 51/3.92 = 13.010 million. your_n = null: this is a modelled global population total, not an analytic sample. The inputs were 17 prevalence studies from 16 countries, extrapolated by a country-imputation algorithm (matching on BMI, race, then geographical proximity) to 177 countries; a denominator sample size is not a meaningful quantity here. UNCERTAINTY CAVEAT: the reported interval reflects sampling uncertainty only, not model uncertainty. The authors' own logistic-regression sensitivity analysis produced a much lower figure for the AHI >= 5 threshold (730 million vs 936 million), so a 399-450 interval almost certainly understates true uncertainty for the 425 million figure. Funded by ResMed. This row is a descriptive disease-burden estimate with no sleep-duration exposure (target_exposure_type='descriptive'), hence normative_descriptive/TX and rob na.
